title: Nachiketa's Doubt
hook: a boy at Death's door is offered every treasure, and keeps asking his one honest question
carry: samshaya: honest doubt opens the search
tomorrow: a starving family gives away its last barley. who was the guest?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden deer and a cry in Rama's voice: hetvabhasa, a reason that only looks real. Today is the last day with Nyaya.
screen: `A REASON THAT ONLY LOOKS REAL.` · `NYAYA, A LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: A father is giving away everything he owns in a great sacrifice, and his young son, Nachiketa, watches the cows go by: old, dry, too tired to give milk. Hardly a gift. So the boy asks: Father, to whom will you give me? No answer. He asks again, and a third time, and his father snaps: to Death! So Nachiketa goes. He waits at the house of Yama, lord of death, three nights without food, because Yama is away. When Yama returns, he's dismayed: a guest, kept waiting. Choose three wishes, he says.
screen: `OLD COWS, A POOR GIFT.` → `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: This is the Katha Upanishad. For his first wish, Nachiketa asks that his father greet him without anger. For the second, to learn a sacred fire. Then the third. When a person dies, he says, there's this doubt: some say he still is, some say he is not. Teach me that. Yama tries to wriggle out. Even the gods doubted this, he says. Ask something else. Sons and grandsons, herds and gold, a long life, music and chariots. Nachiketa says: keep your songs and dances. These last until tomorrow. And because he won't let the question go, Yama teaches him about the atman, the self that is not born and does not die. A whole Upanishad stands on one honest doubt. Centuries later the Nyaya Sutra put doubt, samshaya, near the start of its list of what a seeker must understand: a mind pulled between two possibilities, seeing what they share and not yet what tells them apart. He is; he is not. Vatsyayana, its early commentator, adds that nobody inquires into what is completely unknown, or into what is already settled. Inquiry lives in doubt. Nachiketa doesn't pretend to be sure. He doesn't trade the question for something shinier. He holds it, and asks the one who can answer. That's the teaching, plainly: in Hindu learning, an honest question, carried to the right teacher, is welcome. Doubt is a doorway, not a home. Today the shiny offers are a scroll, a distraction, someone's easy answer. Nachiketa's way is to keep asking.
screen: `HE IS, OR HE IS NOT?` · `KEEP YOUR SONGS AND DANCES.` · `SAMSHAYA: DOUBT STARTS THE SEARCH.` · `A DOORWAY, NOT A HOME.` · then, large: `KEEP ASKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question you honestly can't answer yet, about your life or about God. Name the two sides, the way Nachiketa did: some say this, some say that. Don't rush to pick one. Breathe, and notice what the two share, and what would tell them apart. If you pray, bring the question to God, or to the deity at your home shrine, and wait, the way the boy waited three nights. If you don't, write it down and keep it.
Nyaya. Today, samshaya, doubt: the mind caught between two, where honest inquiry begins.
Your line: samshaya, honest doubt opens the search. Nachiketa kept asking until Death taught him. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families and teachers tell children the story of Nachiketa; in Nyaya study, students meet doubt, samshaya, in the opening list of the Nyaya Sutra, as the place inquiry begins.
